metadata.file_name: 138. Kasap & Köroğlu (2025). The Effect of the Weight Variable on Predicting Reading Comprehension Achievement in PISA 2018: A Data Mining Approach.pdf
metadata.title: The Effect of the Weight Variable on Predicting Reading Comprehension Achievement in PISA 2018: A Data Mining Approach

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 Turkey microdata and constructs models to predict reading comprehension achievement using 34 student-questionnaire variables plus (in one condition) the student-level sampling weight W_FSTUWT (Final Trimmed Nonresponse Adjusted Student). The analytic sample consists of 6,890 students from 186 schools across 12 regions of Turkey, selected via PISA’s multi-stage stratified sampling (schools selected first, then students/classes within schools). The authors explicitly compare weighted vs unweighted analyses by running CART and Random Forest twice: once including W_FSTUWT and once excluding it. Missing data were handled via a multiple assignment method in SPSS, and outliers were checked with no outliers detected; however, the paper does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so uncertainty estimation is not described in replicate-weight terms.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the PISA 2018 Turkey dataset and restricted the analytic sample to 15-year-old students represented by the official Turkey PISA sample: 6,890 students attending 186 schools across 12 regions. The dependent variable was PV1 from the PISA 2018 reading comprehension test, which was then categorized into 'successful' vs 'unsuccessful' using the PISA reading proficiency level table (0–552.999 vs 553–1000). The models used 34 independent variables derived from the PISA 2018 student questionnaire. Outliers were checked and none were detected; missing data were eliminated using SPSS multiple assignment.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Turkey Reading comprehension (PV1; successful vs unsuccessful)
main_findings.target_variable: Reading comprehension achievement category (PV1; successful vs unsuccessful)
main_findings.performance_metrics: CART (10 top variables): PCC 85.755 (weighted) vs 85.887 (unweighted) on all data; Kappa 0.314 (weighted) vs 0.346 (unweighted) on all data. RF (10 top variables): PCC 100 (weighted) vs 100 (unweighted) on all data; Kappa 1 (weighted) vs 1 (unweighted) on all data; on test data Kappa 0.220 (weighted) vs 0.164 (unweighted).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Turkey reading comprehension data (PV1 categorized as successful vs unsuccessful), the study leveraged socioeconomic status (ESCS), perceived test difficulty, parental occupational status, home possessions, and reading enjoyment to predict achievement category using CART and Random Forest, finding that including the student weight variable W_FSTUWT slightly decreased prediction performance but did not significantly reduce overall accuracy. This indicates that incorporating PISA student sampling weights is necessary for valid and reliable variable selection and interpretation, even if predictive accuracy changes only marginally.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 Turkey microdata (6,890 students from 186 schools) to predict reading comprehension achievement using PV1 from the reading test, recoded into a binary 'successful' vs 'unsuccessful' outcome. Using 34 student-questionnaire variables, the authors train CART and Random Forest models in two conditions: with the student-level sampling weight W_FSTUWT and without it. For CART, overall classification/prediction performance remains high and changes only slightly when weights are included (e.g., PCC ~85.8 vs ~85.9 on all data; Kappa decreases from 0.346 to 0.314). For Random Forest, performance is extremely high on all data (PCC and Kappa reported as 100 and 1), while validation/test Kappa is lower and shows differences by weighting (test Kappa 0.220 weighted vs 0.164 unweighted). The paper reports missing-data handling via SPSS multiple assignment and does not describe replicate-weight uncertainty estimation; additionally, the study focuses on predictive performance and variable importance rather than causal effects.
